title: Strategic Partnerships to Secure Critical Resources and Supply Chains
gist: Congressional testimony argues the US cannot achieve critical minerals security without Africa and Central Asia, that China's two-decade infrastructure investment (not just mine ownership) gives it midstream leverage, and that durable, statutorily-anchored US commitments (long-term AGOA, tariff reform, Jackson-Vanik repeal) are the missing lever versus one-to-three-year policy resets.

themes.theme: Africa/Central Asia as indispensable mineral suppliers

insights.claim: The DRC alone supplies about 70 percent of the world's cobalt and has become the world's second-largest copper producer with some of the highest-grade copper deposits globally, while South Africa supplies the vanadium, platinum, palladium, rhodium and chrome that US defense and industrial supply chains quietly depend on.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US defense-industrial supply chain resilience is directly exposed to DRC cobalt and South African PGM concentration risk — a single-country dependency worth tracking for critical minerals investors.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: Kazakhstan is the world's largest uranium producer and a major source of tungsten and chromium, and Central Asia's Trans-Caspian 'Middle Corridor' offers an export route bypassing both Moscow and Beijing, functionally analogous to what the Lobito Corridor does for the Congolese copper belt.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Middle Corridor / Lobito Corridor parallel is a reusable framework for identifying alternative-route infrastructure plays that reduce Chinese/Russian chokepoint leverage over mineral exports.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: Africa's share of global mineral exploration spending fell from 16 percent in 2004 to just over 10 percent in 2024, even though Africa remains the most cost-effective exploration region in the world, delivering more mineral value per exploration dollar than Australia, Canada, or Latin America.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The exploration-spend gap versus superior per-dollar mineral value signals Africa is both underexplored and undervalued — a structural opportunity for exploration-stage capital willing to accept higher country risk.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

themes.theme: China's ecosystem-building strategy vs. mine ownership

insights.claim: Competing in frontier mineral markets requires building the ecosystem around the mine (rail, ports, power, customs systems) not simply developing the orebody itself — China understood this two decades ago and financed the enabling infrastructure through the Belt and Road Initiative.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating African mining juniors should weight surrounding logistics/infrastructure access as heavily as the resource itself — a mine without transport/power access is not bankable regardless of ore grade.
insights.locator: Testimony opening / U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: Chinese companies control the supply chain and global processing capacity for rare earths even though they directly own or operate only a small percentage of African mines, meaning Beijing's leverage comes from midstream (processing/refining) chokepoints rather than upstream ownership.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This reframes the China risk in critical minerals: Western investment in African mine ownership alone does not break Chinese leverage unless matched by Western midstream processing capacity investment.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: China's export restrictions on germanium, gallium, graphite, and antimony demonstrated how mineral dominance translates directly into geopolitical coercion, and Chinese vendors (Huawei, ZTE) built roughly half of Africa's 3G and about 70 percent of its 4G networks, while Chinese AI models and free computing offers are becoming local favorites across the continent.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China's mineral export-control precedent (germanium/gallium/graphite/antimony) is a template for future coercive leverage in other critical minerals — an early-warning framework for supply-chain risk modeling.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: The December 2025 US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement establishes a Strategic Asset Reserve giving US companies a right of first offer on designated mineral projects, and is already moving to deal execution: in February 2026 Glencore signed a non-binding MOU to sell a 40 percent stake in its Mutanda and Kamoto Copper Company mines to the Orion Critical Mineral Consortium, backed by the US DFC and Abu Dhabi's ADQ.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Glencore-Orion-DFC deal is a concrete, trackable transaction testing whether the US-DRC framework converts diplomatic intent into real copper-cobalt equity transfers — a template for future US-backed minerals M&A.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: The State Department's Bureau of African Affairs launched the U.S.-Africa Strategic Investment Program with an estimated $500 million in total funding to accelerate private-sector-led investment in critical minerals and commercial diplomacy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A $500M catalytic program is a concrete near-term funding vehicle for African critical-minerals deal flow to monitor.
insights.locator: The U.S. Critical Minerals Supply Chain Challenge

insights.claim: US partners are committing assets with lives measured in decades while American policy toward them resets in one-to-three-year increments: AGOA lapsed last year, Central Asian partners remain subject to annual Jackson-Vanik waivers, and most critical minerals agreements rely primarily on executive instruments that a future administration can reverse.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This mismatch between decades-long mining investment horizons and 1-3 year US policy cycles is the core structural risk for anyone financing US-backed African/Central Asian mining projects — durability reforms (statutory footing) would materially de-risk these investments.

insights.claim: The Administration has signed more than twenty critical minerals frameworks, MOUs, and strategic agreements in the past year (including with DRC, Guinea, Morocco, and Uzbekistan), but most depend substantially on executive-branch authority and can be reversed or modified by a future administration since Congress had no defined role in negotiating them.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors relying on these 20+ agreements as durable policy backstops should recognize the political-reversal risk and watch for the recommended statutory codification as a de-risking catalyst.

insights.claim: Congress should write a ten-year AGOA reauthorization rather than the current two-year extension to 2028, because a mine or rail line financed today will not generate revenue until the 2030s and investors will not build around a program that resets every two or three years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 10-year AGOA reauthorization would be a significant de-risking catalyst for African infrastructure/mining investment; its passage or failure over the next two years is a key policy signpost.

themes.theme: Tariff policy penalizes the value addition it claims to encourage

insights.claim: Refined copper cathode from the DRC or Zambia carries only a 1 percent MFN duty and may enter the US duty-free under AGOA, but when a Zambian or Congolese producer converts that copper into rod, wire, tube, or sheet, those higher-value products face a 50 percent Section 232 tariff — assessed since April 6, 2026 on the full customs value rather than just the copper content.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This tariff escalation structurally punishes exactly the downstream value-addition the US claims to want, creating a perverse incentive for African producers to keep exporting raw ore — a specific, fixable policy failure investors in African copper processing should watch for reform.
insights.locator: Ensure U.S. tariff policy rewards, rather than penalizes, mineral value addition

insights.claim: The Administration is considering a universal tariff on refined copper of 15 percent beginning in 2027 and 30 percent beginning in 2028, which could affect the very refined copper exports that US investments in the Lobito Corridor are intended to bring to American markets.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 2027-2028 universal refined-copper tariff would directly undercut the commercial case for Lobito Corridor-linked copper exports — a policy risk that could strand US-backed infrastructure investment.
insights.locator: Ensure U.S. tariff policy rewards, rather than penalizes, mineral value addition

themes.theme: Cold War-era trade law as a live obstacle

insights.claim: Congress should consider repealing Jackson-Vanik (enacted in 1974 to pressure the Soviet Union over emigration restrictions) for Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and other Central Asian partners, since maintaining a Cold War-era trade restriction sends a signal of unreliability precisely as the US courts these countries as strategic minerals partners.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Jackson-Vanik repeal is a low-cost, high-signal legislative action that could unlock deeper US investment commitments in Central Asian uranium/copper/rare earth projects.
insights.locator: Consider repealing Jackson-Vanik for U.S. strategic partners in Central Asia
